content: Mimosa pudica, commonly known as the Sensitive Plant, is a creeping herbaceous plant that can be either annual or perennial. It is often cultivated for its unique and fascinating behavior: its compound leaves fold inward and droop when touched, only to reopen within minutes. This plant is native to Brazil but has become a pantropical weed, spreading across various regions of the world. The plant is known by several other names, including Humble Plant, Tickle Me Plant, Shame Plant, Sleeping Grass, Prayer Plant, and Touch-me-not. In the Philippines, it is called Makahiya, which translates to shy, while in the West Indies, it is referred to as Mori Vivi, and in Tonga, it is known as mate-loi, meaning false death. Its Chinese name translates to shyness grass. The species epithet pudica is derived from Latin, meaning bashful or shrinking, reflecting its unique response to stimuli and its ease of propagation. In Sinhala, it is called Nidikumba, where nidi means sleep. The seeds of this plant are marketed to children under the name Tickle Me Plant. In its early stages, the stem of Mimosa pudica is erect, but as the plant matures, it becomes creeping or trailing, reaching lengths of up to 5 meters (approximately 5 feet). The leaves are bipinnately compound, with one or two pairs of pinnae and 10–26 leaflets per pinna. The petioles are prickly. The plant produces pale pink or purple flower heads that are pedunculate (stalked) and arise from the leaf axils. These globose to ovoid flower heads measure 8–10 mm in diameter, excluding the stamens. Upon closer inspection, the florets reveal red petals in their upper parts and filaments that range in color from pink to lavender. The fruit consists of clusters of 2–8 pods, each 1–2 cm long, with prickly margins. Mimosa pudica is renowned for its rapid plant movements. In the evening, its leaflets fold together, and the entire leaf droops downward, reopening at sunrise. This phenomenon is classified as nyctinastic movement. Additionally, the leaves close in response to various stimuli, such as touch, warming, or shaking. The stimulus can also be transmitted to neighboring leaves, a type of movement known as seismonastic movement. These movements are caused by a rapid loss of turgor pressure in specific cells, leading to the drooping of leaves. In traditional medicine, particularly Ayurveda, Mimosa pudica is identified as the plant Lajjalu. It is described as a plant that folds its leaves upon touch and reopens them after some time. The plant is characterized by its bitter and astringent taste and has been historically used to treat various ailments. While the root is most commonly utilized, other parts of the plant, including the leaves, flowers, bark, and fruit, are also employed for medicinal purposes. In Ayurveda, the properties (guna) of Lajjalu include: A bitter (tikta) and astringent (kashaya) taste. A cooling property (sheetha). The ability to balance the kapha and pitta doshas. It is classified by Sushruta in the Priyangwambhastadi gana group. In cultivation, Mimosa pudica is often grown as an indoor annual plant but is also used as ground cover. Propagation is typically achieved through seeds.
